nameStory: The Black-staining Polypore gets its name from a very distinctive trait - when you touch or bruise this mushroom, it turns dramatically black! The word 'polypore' refers to its underside structure of tiny pores instead of gills, like thousands of microscopic tubes where spores are released.
description: This is a large, bracket-like fungus that grows in overlapping, fan-shaped clusters at the base of trees. The caps are typically brown to grayish-brown with a somewhat fuzzy or velvety surface when young. It can form impressive clusters that may span several feet across, with individual caps reaching 4-12 inches wide. The underside is white to cream-colored and covered in tiny pores rather than gills.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Touch any part of the mushroom and watch it turn black within minutes - this is the signature feature that makes identification nearly foolproof

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Brown to grayish-brown caps that feel somewhat velvety or fuzzy when young, growing in overlapping, fan-shaped clusters

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Tiny white to cream-colored pores on the underside that also turn black when touched or bruised

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms large, impressive clusters at the base of trees with multiple overlapping brackets growing from a shared base

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Often has a slightly sweet or pleasant mushroomy smell when fresh, becoming more pungent as it ages

habitat: Look for Black-staining Polypore at the base of hardwood trees, especially oaks and maples, throughout New England's forests. It grows as a parasite and saprophyte, often appearing where trees are stressed or dying. You'll typically find it in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges from lowlands to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins to emerge as temperatures warm, appearing as small, fresh brackets that are especially velvety to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fresh, actively growing specimens showing the most dramatic black-staining reaction when touched.
seasonality.fall: Mature specimens are most common and easiest to spot, though they may be tougher and less reactive to bruising than summer finds.
seasonality.winter: Old, weathered specimens may persist but become tough and woody, often losing the distinctive black-staining characteristic.

funFact: This mushroom is like nature's ink pad - indigenous peoples and modern foragers have actually used the black staining as a natural dye and even for writing, as the black color is quite permanent once it develops!
confusionNotes: It's sometimes confused with Hen-of-the-Woods (Maitake), which also grows in clusters at tree bases, but Hen-of-the-Woods has a more frilly, layered appearance and doesn't turn black when touched. Remember: if it doesn't stain black, it's not a Black-staining Polypore!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'giant polypore' in some regions, this name can be confusing since several other large polypores exist. Always use the black-staining characteristic as your primary identifier rather than relying on size alone.
compareHints: The Black-staining Polypore is easily distinguished from its relatives by the dramatic black bruising reaction. While other Meripilus species may show some color changes when damaged, none exhibit the immediate and intense black staining that makes M. sumstinei so distinctive. This bruising reaction is so reliable that it's considered the definitive field characteristic for this species.
